1205.title: The Gatha of Guru Arjan
1205.hook: a short, dense poem in an old literary style (ang 1360)
1205.howItsDone: The Gatha of Guru Arjan is read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib's closing sections; because of its old literary vocabulary, some Sikhs study it with a giani or a teeka, line by line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sehskriti's warnings: katanch, where is mother, where is father. Your line was passing things.

A spoonful of honey and a glass of sugar water can hold the same sweetness. One you sip for a while. The other you taste all at once, and it stays on the tongue. On Ang thirteen hundred sixty of the Guru Granth Sahib sits a short composition by Guru Arjan called the Gatha. It's the honey: short, packed, written in an old literary style, every line carrying more than its size suggests. You don't read it quickly. You let it sit on the tongue.
screen: `HONEY AND SUGAR WATER.` → `ANG 1360.` → `LET IT SIT ON THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Gatha is often glossed as a verse or a song, and here it's the heading of the composition itself. It's short and dense, in an old literary style. Like the Sehskriti, its words carry an older, learned sound, so some Sikhs study it with someone who knows the vocabulary. Its opening lines, paraphrased: camphor, flowers and perfume, touching the human body, become soiled. That's a startling start. Most of us think of the body as the thing that needs perfume, and here the perfume is what gets dirty. Read on, and the Gatha keeps pointing past the body's surface: to the Name, the company of the holy, the Lord's praise. Each line works like a seed, small enough to hold in your palm, holding a whole tree. That's what dense means. Not difficult for its own sake, but folded, so it opens slowly. A long hymn can carry you along by its flow. A dense one asks you to stop: read a phrase, put it down, look at it from another side. A reader can come back to a single line for days. Some truths arrive in a flood of words. Others come in a spoonful, and the work is to let them dissolve.

segments.voice: If you can find the Gatha on Ang thirteen hundred sixty, read only its first line, in Gurmukhi or in translation; if not, take today's paraphrase: camphor and flowers, touching the body, become soiled. Close your eyes, let the line sit, and turn it over once to see what surprises you. One line, all the way down.
Gatha. A verse, a song; Guru Arjan's short, dense composition in an old literary style on Ang thirteen hundred sixty. Today's word.
Your line: dense and short. A small line can hold a whole tree. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1206.title: The Funhe verses
1206.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Funhe are read as part of the closing sections of the Guru Granth Sahib, and some are sung in kirtan, where the refrain har haan gives the singing its pulse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gatha, Guru Arjan's spoonful of honey. Your line was dense and short.

Har haan. Two syllables, like a foot coming down at the turn of a dance step. Har haan. Right after the Gatha, on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-one, come Guru Arjan's Funhe, short verses that each turn on that same small refrain. Yesterday was density, one line folded tight. Today is rhythm, the same beat returning verse after verse, the way a heart keeps time. And what that heart keeps time for, it turns out, is someone it misses.
screen: `HAR HAAN.` → `RIGHT AFTER THE GATHA.` → `THE SAME BEAT RETURNING.`

segments.voice: The Funhe are short rhythmic verses of longing, and both halves matter. First, the rhythm. In each verse, the last line opens with har haan, a refrain some explain as the Lord's name with a sung affirmation, something like yes, Lord. Because it comes back every time, the verses have a pulse you can feel before you follow the meaning. Then, the longing. They open with an image, paraphrased: with pen in hand, the Inaccessible One writes on the forehead. From there the verses keep reaching toward the Beloved: the Lord's beauty, the wish to meet, the sweetness of the holy company where the Name is sung. They're short enough that the longing never becomes a speech. It just keeps arriving, beat by beat. Why would longing want a rhythm? Missing someone works like this. It doesn't come once and leave. It comes back on its own schedule: at the kettle, at the door, at the same hour each night. The Funhe give that returning a shape and a direction. Instead of a wound that reopens, the return becomes a refrain, a place the heart keeps landing on purpose. Seen this way, a repeating line in kirtan isn't filler. It's the heart finding its footing, again.
screen: `A REFRAIN IN EVERY VERSE.` · `THE PEN ON THE FOREHEAD.` · `LONGING THAT KEEPS ARRIVING.` · `A RETURN WITH A DIRECTION.` · then, large: `RHYTHMIC LONGING.`

segments.voice: If you can find the Funhe on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-one, read three of them slowly, and let your voice drop a little on every har haan, like a step landing. If not, let the breath be the rhythm: in, and on the out-breath, the two syllables, quietly, har haan. Don't force a feeling; just let the beat come back, and notice what it reaches for.
The Funhe verses. Guru Arjan's short verses of longing, each one landing on the refrain har haan. Today's word.
Your line: rhythmic longing. Har haan, and the heart lands home again. See you tomorrow.

1207.title: The Chaubole verses
1207.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Chaubole are read among the closing sections of the Guru Granth Sahib; gianis may explain them in katha, including the verse about a love that money cannot buy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Funhe, landing again and again on har haan. Your line was rhythmic longing.

What would you pay for love? It's an odd question until someone actually tries. A ring that costs too much. A trip meant to fix things. A gift that arrives instead of a person. On Ang thirteen hundred sixty-three, just past the Funhe, Guru Arjan's Chaubole take up that question. They speak of love, calling out to listeners by name. And the first thing they say is about money, and what it can't do.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU PAY FOR LOVE?` → `ANG 1363.` → `WHAT MONEY CAN'T DO.`

segments.voice: The name is often heard as chau, four, and bole, things spoken: four sayings, or four voices. Readers explain the four in different ways, and the text doesn't stop to say. What's clear is the subject: love, prem, the love of the soul for the Lord. The verses call out to people by name, Samman and Musan among them, as if the Guru were turning to friends in a circle. Here's one, paraphrased. Samman, if this love could be bought with money, think of Ravan, the king of the old epic. He was no pauper, the verse says, and he gave his own heads, yet he could not buy it. That's the turn: a king with treasure to spare, willing to give even his own heads, still couldn't purchase it. Love of this kind isn't a sale. Other verses, paraphrased again, speak of love spread like moonlight across the sky, and of the bumblebee caught fast in the lotus it loves. Four voices can also mean something simple and human: love gets talked about from more than one side. The one who longs, the one who's asked, the friend who watches, the Beloved who's silent. One voice would make it a lecture. Several make it a conversation, and it keeps coming back to the same discovery: what the soul wants most can't be bought, only given and received.
screen: `CHAU, FOUR; BOLE, SAYINGS.` · `CALLING OUT TO SAMMAN.` · `RAVAN COULDN'T BUY IT.` · `LOVE FROM MORE THAN ONE SIDE.` · then, large: `FOUR VOICES.`

segments.voice: If you can find the Chaubole on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-three, read one verse and notice who it's speaking to. If not, hold someone you love in mind and let four voices take a turn in silence: what you'd say to them, what they might say back, what a friend watching would say, and the quiet underneath. Then let the breath settle.
The Chaubole verses. Guru Arjan's verses on love, often heard as four sayings, calling out to listeners by name. Today's word.
Your line: four voices. Even Ravan's treasure couldn't buy it. Same time tomorrow.

1208.title: The plate of three things
1208.hook: on this plate are three things, truth, contentment and reflection, the seal on the Granth (Mundavani, ang 1429)
1208.tomorrow: The Lord stood to finish the work
1208.howItsDone: Sikhs read the Mundavani as part of the bhog, the completion of a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and its opening line about the plate of three things is often explained in katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chaubole: love that even a king couldn't buy. Your line was four voices.

A steel plate, a thaal, set down on a cloth. In a Sikh home or a gurdwara you might see one holding karah prashad, or food for a guest. Now turn to Ang fourteen hundred twenty-nine, near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Guru Arjan sets down a plate of his own and tells you exactly what's on it. Not sweets, not bread. Three things, and then a fourth that holds the others up. It's the Mundavani, and it comes near the close of the Granth like a seal on a letter.
screen: `A STEEL PLATE ON A CLOTH.` → `ANG 1429.` → `A SEAL ON A LETTER.`

segments.voice: You met this plate before, at the Granth's four-hundredth year; today, a closer look. Here it is, paraphrased. On this plate, three things have been placed: truth, contentment and reflection. The nectar of the Lord's Name has been placed here too, the support of all. Whoever eats it, whoever enjoys it, is saved. This can't be given up; keep it always in your heart. The dark world-ocean is crossed by holding to the Lord's feet; Nanak, all of this is the Lord's own spreading out. Mundavani is often explained as a seal, the kind pressed into wax to close a letter. So near its close, the Granth names what was inside it all along. Take the three one at a time. Sat, truth: not only telling the truth, but living close to what's real. Santokh, contentment: enough, the end of the endless more. Vichar, reflection: turning the teaching over in the mind. Then the Name, amrit naam, laid beside them as the thing everything rests on. Notice the verbs: eat, enjoy, keep it in your heart. This plate isn't for a shelf. It's a meal. Sikhs read the Mundavani at the completion of a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, so a long reading ends at a table: truth to stand on, enough to rest in, reflection to grow by, and the Name to feed them.

segments.voice: Set out any plate and three small things nearby, a coin, a key, a leaf, and lay them down one at a time, naming each: truth, contentment, reflection. Then sit with the plate in front of you and ask quietly which of the three your day needs most, without trying to solve anything. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you look.

1209.title: The Lord stood to finish the work
1209.word: The Lord stood to finish the work
1209.hook: the Lord Himself stood to complete the saints' task, sung of the pool at Amritsar (Suhi M5, ang 783)
1209.howItsDone: This hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Suhi is sung in kirtan, and some Sikhs connect it with the sarovar at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar and with seva done there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mundavani, the plate that seals the Granth. Your line was truth, contentment, reflection.

Dig a hole by hand and there comes a moment. Shovel after shovel, the pile grows, and the hole seems to shrink. Then someone climbs down beside you and takes the other end. In Raga Suhi, on Ang seven hundred eighty-three, Guru Arjan sings about a great work of digging and building: the pool at Amritsar, the work tradition says his father, Guru Ram Das, began. And the song doesn't say, look what we built. It says something stranger. The Lord stood up to do it.
screen: `SHOVEL AFTER SHOVEL.` → `THE POOL AT AMRITSAR.` → `THE LORD STOOD UP TO DO IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, paraphrased: for the task of the saints, the Lord Himself stood up; He came to have the work done. Khaloiaa, stood up, is a picture word. Not watching from far off, not sending help: standing, the way a person gets up when the work in front of them matters. The hymn goes on, again paraphrased: the land is beautiful, the pool is beautiful, filled with nectar water. Sikh tradition sings it of the pool at Amritsar, around which the Harmandir Sahib stands. Now look at who gets the credit. Tradition remembers builders and diggers and the sangat carrying earth: real people doing real labor. The hymn doesn't deny it. It just says whose hand was underneath theirs. The saints had the task; the Lord stood to finish it. This path has been circling the same idea. The Bavan Akhri ended in grace. The Mundavani laid the Name on the plate as the support of all. Here the same truth wears work clothes, dusty, with a shovel. Effort is honored, and then the one who completes it is named. Some readers hear in this hymn permission to be finished: not because you got it all done alone, but because you weren't alone in it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one task you've been carrying alone, half-dug, and sit with it a moment. Ask honestly who could take the other end of the shovel: a friend, a coworker, someone in your family. If you pray, hold the task before Waheguru and leave it there for a breath.
The Lord stood to finish the work. For the saints' task, Guru Arjan sings, the Lord Himself stood up; sung of the pool at Amritsar. Today's word.

1210.title: Your doing is sweet
1210.hook: tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do seems sweet to me (Asa M5, ang 394)
1210.howItsDone: Tera keeaa meethaa laagai is sung in kirtan and repeated by Sikhs as a short line of acceptance; it is often recalled in remembrance of Guru Arjan's martyrdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord stood up to finish the saints' work at the pool. Your line was he finished it.

Tera keeaa meethaa laagai. Four words in Punjabi, short enough to say in a single breath, before a meeting or at a hospital door. In Raga Asa, on Ang three hundred ninety-four, Guru Arjan says them plainly: what You do seems sweet to me. Hear it once and it sounds gentle. Hear it on a hard day and it sounds almost impossible. That gap between the gentle and the impossible is where today's line lives.
screen: `TERA KEEAA MEETHAA LAAGAI.` → `ASA, ANG 394.` → `GENTLE, OR IMPOSSIBLE?`

segments.voice: Back on day sixty-four, tradition placed these words in Lahore; today, the line itself. Here's the couplet, paraphrased: what You do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Lord's Name. Take the words one at a time. Tera, yours. Keeaa, the doing. Meethaa, sweet. Laagai, it seems, it strikes me as. Notice that last word. The Guru doesn't say everything that happens is pleasant. He says how it lands on him. Sweetness here is a way of receiving, not a weather report. And notice the second half. The request isn't for a better outcome. It's for the Name: not change what's happening, but give me the treasure that lets me meet it. That's the heart of what Sikhs call bhana, the Lord's will, and accepting it. It's easy to mishear. Accepting the will isn't shrugging at injustice; Sikh teaching also speaks of standing up to wrong. It's more like a settled place inside, from which a person can act without bitterness. Sikh tradition recalls this line alongside Guru Arjan's last days in Lahore, when, tradition says, he was tortured and killed under the Mughal authorities, and met that suffering steadily, remembering the One. And accepting the will never means accepting harm: if someone is hurting you, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `TERA, KEEAA, MEETHAA, LAAGAI.` · `HOW IT LANDS, NOT THE WEATHER.` · `ASKING FOR THE NAME, NOT AN OUTCOME.` · `BHANA: ACCEPTING THE WILL.` · then, large: `YOUR WILL IS SWEET.`

segments.voice: Choose something small that didn't go your way this week, a delay, a plan that changed, and let it be what it is for a moment without arguing. On the in-breath, tera keeaa; on the out-breath, meethaa laagai. If the sweetness doesn't come, that's all right; just notice the place inside where it might, and if you pray, ask for the Name, as the line does.
Your doing is sweet. Tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do seems sweet to me, and Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name. Today's word.

1211.title: No fast, no Ramadan: the One served
1211.hook: Guru Arjan sings that he keeps no fast of one faith or the other but serves the One alone (Bhairao M5, ang 1136)
1211.carry: one master, called gosain and allah
1211.howItsDone: This hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Bhairao is often quoted when Sikhs explain their path as distinct and devoted to the One; in the gurdwara it is sung in kirtan and explained in katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do seems sweet. Your line was your will is sweet.

A street in Lahore or Amritsar in Guru Arjan's day. One neighbor is keeping a Hindu fast. Another is keeping the fast of Ramadan. Both are serious, both devout, and both might well ask the Guru's Sikhs: so which do you keep? In Raga Bhairao, on Ang eleven hundred thirty-six, Guru Arjan answers. He doesn't mock either fast, and he doesn't pick one. He names, instead, whom he serves.
screen: `TWO NEIGHBORS, TWO FASTS.` → `WHICH DO YOU KEEP?` → `HE NAMES WHOM HE SERVES.`

segments.voice: On day six, the question was whether Sikhs are Hindu or Muslim; here a Guru answers in a hymn. Its opening, paraphrased: I keep no fast, nor the month of Ramadan; I serve the One who protects me in the end. And then: the one Master, Gosain and Allah, is mine. Gosain is a name for God from Hindu speech; Allah is the name in Muslim speech. The Guru uses both, for one Lord. The hymn goes on to say he doesn't go on pilgrimage to Mecca or worship at Hindu holy places, and later, paraphrased: I am neither Hindu nor Muslim; my body and breath belong to Allah and Ram. It's easy to hear this as a rejection. Read in its setting, it's a statement of where the Guru stands: not against his neighbors, not ranking their devotion, but naming a path given wholly to the One, whatever name the One is called by. Sevi, I serve, is the working word. Service, seva, runs through the Gurus' teaching, and the hymn makes the One the only master of that service. This week has followed one thread in different clothes: the Gatha, the Funhe, the Chaubole, the Mundavani's plate, the Lord standing up to finish the work, a will received as sweet. And now, the One served by all of it. Different forms, one direction.
screen: `NO FAST, NO RAMADAN.` · `GOSAIN AND ALLAH, ONE MASTER.` · `NEITHER HINDU NOR MUSLIM.` · `THE WEEK, ONE DIRECTION.` · then, large: `SERVING THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind whoever or whatever your life is most given to: for some it's God, for some a child, a parent, a calling. Hold that one in your attention and let a small service you could offer come to you, a chore, a call, a quiet act of care, without chasing it. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each out-breath.
Serving the One. Guru Arjan's hymn in Raga Bhairao: no fast of one faith or the other; I serve the One who protects me in the end. Today's word.
Your line: one Master, called Gosain and Allah. That closes a week of Guru Arjan's shorter forms and his seal. Rest well.
